Rabbi Ovadia Hedaya: Between the Revealed and the Hidden at the Threshold of Redemption

The text surveys the life history and doctrine of Rabbi Ovadia Hedaya, who was among the foremost halakhic decisors and kabbalists of the twentieth century and served as a bridge between the old Torah world of Aleppo and the emerging Israeli reality. The author emphasizes the unique structure of his central work, Yaskil Avdi, which synthetically integrates the revealed Torah with the mystical depth of Kabbalah, while addressing technological and modern issues. The chapters of the article describe his public activity as a judge in the Supreme Rabbinical Court and as one who restored the kabbalists' yeshiva Beit El after the destruction of the Old City, thereby ensuring the continuity of the spiritual leadership dynasty. Finally, the source highlights his Zionist-kabbalistic conception, which saw in the establishment of the State of Israel an essential stage in the process of redemption, and explains how his legacy continues to influence the character of the Sephardic rabbinate in our day.

The Torah Doctrine and Public Work of Rabbi Ovadia Hedaya: Between the Revealed and the Hidden at the Threshold of Redemption

Processes of Formation and Growth: The Roots of the Hedaya Family and the Aleppan-Jerusalemite Connection

The figure of Rabbi Ovadia Hedaya represents one of the most impressive and significant chapters in the history of the Sephardic rabbinate and halakhic-kabbalistic thought in the twentieth century. Investigation of his work requires deep understanding of the cultural and spiritual space in which he grew, a space that combines the stringent and precise tradition of the sages of Aram Tzova (Aleppo) with the mystical depth of the kabbalists of Yeshivat Beit El in Jerusalem. The Rabbi was born in the month of Kislev 5650 (late December 1889) in the city of Aleppo in the Ottoman Empire, to a family that was steeped in generations of Torah and rabbinical jurisprudence.[1, 2] His father, Rabbi Shalom Hedaya, was an exemplary figure who served as a critical connecting link between the old world and the new; he was known as great in both the revealed Torah and the hidden Torah, and even though he suffered from blindness, he continued to serve as a judge in Jerusalem and later as head of the kabbalists' yeshiva Beit El.[3]

The family's move to the Land of Israel in the year 5658 (1898) was not accidental, but stemmed from a combination of medical need and religious longing. His father first went to Alexandria for eye surgery, but the journey ended in immigration to Jerusalem, a step that shaped the future of the young Rabbi Ovadia.[1] In Jerusalem, Rabbi Ovadia was absorbed into the educational institutions of the Sephardic community, from the Talmud Torah "Doresh Zion" to the yeshivot "Hesed Avraham" and "Tiferet Yerushalayim".[1, 2] His early education was characterized by a synthesis between study of the plain meaning and the tradition of the secret, as his father hired for him the kabbalist Rabbi Shalom Bukhbut as a private teacher for the foundations of Kabbalah already at age 17.[1, 2] His spiritual development was also greatly influenced by the kabbalists Rabbi Yitzhak Sarim and Rabbi Yitzhak Alfiya, who instilled in him the unique approach of the sages of the East: an inseparable integration between practical halakha and kabbalistic depth.[1]

Rabbi Hedaya's family foundations provide a rare glimpse into the Torah network of connections of that period. On his mother's side, Rabbanit Sarah, he was the grandson of Rabbi Yitzhak Lavaton, and on his father's side the grandson of Rabbi Moshe Hayyim Hedaya.[2] These connections were expanded through his marriage to Rabbanit Tzalha (Shulamit), daughter of Rabbi Ezra Sarim, a step that connected him to the elite Torah families of Aleppan emigrants in Jerusalem.[1, 2] During the period of World War I, the Rabbi found himself in a complex political reality; in order to avoid conscription into the Turkish army, he fled back to his birthplace Aleppo for four years, where he continued to deepen in Torah far from the tumult of the battles of the Land of Israel.[1]

Major Milestones in His Life History

Torah Leadership at Yeshivat Porat Yosef and in the Petah Tikva Community

With the establishment of Yeshivat "Porat Yosef" in the Old City in the year 5683, Rabbi Hedaya became one of the dominant figures in teaching the revealed and the hidden. His role as rosh metivta was not limited to transmission of knowledge alone, but included comprehensive spiritual guidance in the spirit of the sages of the East. He was particularly active in Yeshivat "Oz veHadar" which operated within the framework of Porat Yosef, where he led the prayers according to the intentions of the Ari.[1] Testimony to his spiritual mortification and devotion can be found in reports about his functioning as prayer leader on Yom Kippur, when he stood on his feet from sunrise until the Ne'ila prayer without interruption, completely focused on the intentions of prayer and detached from bodily fatigue.[2]

In the year 5699 (1939), his public sphere of activity expanded with his appointment as chief Sephardic rabbi of Petah Tikva. His tenure in this city, which lasted about 12 years, was a test period for his ability to lead a community undergoing processes of modernization and secularization within the new yishuv.[1, 2] In Petah Tikva the Rabbi functioned not only as a halakhic decisor, but as a communal leader who preached in synagogues and brought the public closer to tradition. His success in this role paved his way to the Chief Rabbinical Council and the Supreme Rabbinical Court of Appeals in Jerusalem, to which he was appointed in 1951.[1, 6] His position in the Supreme Court placed him at the forefront of the halakhic decisions of the young state, where he was required to apply his immense expertise in the Talmud and the halakhic decisors to complex social and personal issues.

Public Positions and Judicial Authorities

Halakhic Phenomenology: The Responsa "Yaskil Avdi" as a Nexus of Revealed and Hidden

Rabbi Hedaya's monumental literary enterprise centers on the eight volumes of responsa (she'elot u-teshuvot) Yaskil Avdi. This work is not merely a collection of halakhic rulings, but an expression of a unique methodology that integrates the different realms of Torah knowledge. In each volume the Rabbi was careful to add a section called "De'ah veHaskel," dedicated to questions and answers in the hidden Torah, which emphasizes his conception that halakha and Kabbalah draw from the same divine root.[2, 3] His rulings are characterized by intellectual independence and broad-ranging knowledge, which made him an address for questioners from all parts of the Jewish world, including Ashkenazic communities in Poland, Lithuania, and Hungary.[2]

In his books Rabbi Hedaya addressed many technological and modern issues, among them questions pertaining to electricity, radio, and innovative medical equipment. His approach was examining and penetrating; he did not hasten to forbid or permit, but analyzed the new physical reality from the sources of the Talmud and the halakhic decisors.[7] In addition to responsa, he composed the books Eved HaMelekh on Maimonides, Avda DeRabbanan on the Talmud, and VaYikah Ovadyahu on homiletics, names that express his worldview as a "servant of God" who dedicates his entire being to clarification of Torah truth.[2] In the year 5728 he received official recognition for his enterprise when he was awarded the Israel Prize for Torah literature, this after winning the Rabbi Kook Prize in the year 5719.[1]

Yeshivat Beit El: Preservation of Tradition within Destruction and Revival

The story of the kabbalists' yeshiva "Beit El" under Rabbi Hedaya's leadership is a parable for the revival of the Jewish spirit in Jerusalem. The yeshiva, originally founded in the Old City and a center for the greatest kabbalists (among them the Rashash and the Hida), underwent severe upheaval in the War of Independence. With the fall of the Jewish Quarter in the year 5708, the yeshiva building was destroyed and Rabbi Hedaya was forced to find alternative ways to continue its activity.[2, 3] After his father's death in 5705, he was appointed head of the yeshiva, and in the year 5714 (1954) he began the operation to restore it in the new Jerusalem.[3, 4]

Initially the institution operated in the Midrash Matalon synagogue, but in the year 5718 (1958) the Rabbi dedicated the new building of the yeshiva above the roof of his private home in the Yegi'a Kapayim neighborhood (Rashi Street). The building, adorned with an impressive dome, became a spiritual center where the mekhuvanim continued to pray and study according to the "Beit El" tradition.[3, 4] In order to ensure the future of the Torah world, he also established in the same location Yeshivat "Shalom Avdo" for study of the revealed, out of an understanding that Kabbalah cannot exist without a solid foundation of plain meaning and halakha.[3, 6] After his death in 5729, the yeshiva continued to operate under the leadership of his son, Rabbi Shalom Mordekhai Hayyim Hedaya, and his grandson, Rabbi Rafael Hedaya.[3]

# Zionist-Kabbalistic Orientation: The State as the Beginning of Redemption

One of the most fascinating aspects of Rabbi Hadaya's personality was his positive and active relationship with the Zionist movement and the establishment of the State of Israel. In contrast to segments of his colleagues on the Council of Torah Sages or in certain circles in Jerusalem, Rabbi Hadaya viewed the modern return to Zion as an event possessing profound mystical significance. He argued that the success of the Zionist enterprise, despite its being largely secular, constituted proof of "heavenly assistance," since nothing comes into being in the lower world without approval and consent in the supernal worlds.[6] According to his doctrine, the Holy One, blessed be He, showed Adam the first man all the history of Israel, including the establishment of the state and its leaders, and therefore they must be regarded as instruments in the comprehensive divine plan.[6]

The rabbi defined the period as "athalta de-geula" (the beginning of redemption), a concept he employed to encourage aliyah to the Land and to strengthen the hands of the settlers. He confronted courageously the issue of the "three oaths" (the midrash prohibiting active aliyah and rebellion against the nations), and argued—relying on the Zohar and on the words of the Hida—that the validity of the oaths expired after one thousand years of exile.[6] Consequently, in the generation of the kabbalist, there obtained a religious obligation to work actively for redemption. He even proposed an original interpretation of the sins of the generation: relying on the words of Rabbi Abraham Azulai, he argued that one whom the Land does not vomit out is considered righteous in a certain sense, and therefore myriads of immigrants merit spiritual rectification by the very fact of their dwelling in the Land.[6]

# The Connection with Chabad Hasidism and the Lubavitcher Rebbe

A further dimension revealed in recent scholarship is the profound Torah connection between Rabbi Hadaya and the Lubavitcher Rebbe, Rabbi Menachem Mendel Schneerson. The connection found expression in an exchange of letters and in enormous mutual esteem. In a letter from the year 5719 (1959), the Rebbe thanked Rabbi Hadaya for sending the fifth volume of "Yaskil Avdi" and noted with praise the integration of revealed and hidden Torah, an integration consonant with the method of Hasidism.[3] The Rebbe encouraged Rabbi Hadaya to establish regular classes in Hasidic works, relying on the words of the Ari that in these generations it is a commandment to reveal the wisdom of the hidden.[3]

The use of exalted appellations such as "rav po'alim yoshev al midin" on the part of the Rebbe attests to the international standing of Rabbi Hadaya as a posek and as a kabbalist.[3] The exchange of books and Torah annotations in the margins reflects a dialogue between two kabbalistic schools—the Sephardic-Jerusalemite and the Hasidic-Chabad—which found a common language in the struggle to disseminate the wellsprings of Torah outward and to hasten the redemption.

# Legacy and Students: Shaping the Face of Sephardic Rabbinate in the Next Generation

The influence of Rabbi Ovadiah Hadaya was not confined to his books alone, but was disseminated through his students who became central spiritual leaders. The two most prominent students are Rabbi Mordechai Eliyahu, later Rishon LeZion and Chief Rabbi of Israel, and Rabbi Meir Yehudah Getz, who was rabbi of the Western Wall.[1, 6] These students imbibed from him the unique integration of halakhic precision with kabbalistic depth and unconditional love of Israel. Rabbi Eliyahu, for example, continued his teacher's path in legal rulings that incorporate the words of the kabbalists, while Rabbi Getz continued the mission of rehabilitating Yeshivat Beit El in the Old City after the Six-Day War.[4, 8]

His spiritual figure was portrayed as one who unites opposites: a strict judge in the Great Rabbinical Court together with a pious and humble man in his prayer.[2] His passing on Shabbat, 20 Shevat 5729, at the time of Minhah—a time considered in kabbalah to be the time of re'uta de-re'utin (the will of wills)—was perceived by his disciples as a symbolic conclusion to the life of a man who was cleaving to the supernal worlds while acting in this world.[2] He was interred on Har HaMenuhot in Jerusalem, leaving behind a legacy of complete Torah that unites the plain meaning and the esoteric, state and sanctity.

# His Central Torah Works

# Summary and Assessment of His Achievement

Rabbi Ovadiah Hadaya was a bridge figure in a period of tremendous historical transformations. He succeeded in preserving the distinctiveness of the Sephardic-halakhic and kabbalistic-Jerusalemite tradition, while giving it a modern face relevant to the reality of a sovereign state. His Zionist-kabbalistic approach supplied profound religious legitimation to the national movement, and his halakhic rulings in the responsa "Yaskil Avdi" constitute to this day an inexhaustible source for scholars and decisors. His work in rehabilitating Yeshivat Beit El and training the future generation of the rabbinate in Israel ensure that his name will be remembered as one of the great figures of Torah and spirit who arose for the people of Israel in the generation of revival. In his writing and leadership, the rabbi realized his aspiration to be "the servant of the King"—faithful to his sources, devoted to his people, and looking toward a future of complete redemption.
